OPPOSITION OF DEFENDANTS KATIE HALL, ESQ. &
THE NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN
TO PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE SECOND AMENDED COMPLAINT

Defendants Katie Hall, Esq. and the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children
[collectively, “NCMEC”], by and through undersigned counsel and pursuant to the Rules and
Orders of this Honorable Court, hereby respectfully opposes Plaintiffs “Motion for Leave to File
Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint and Request for Expedited Determination on the
Papers” [Doc. 59]. Plaintiff’s Motion should be denied, on the basis of futility, because Plaintiff
did not comply with the Court’s Order to provide a redline version, and because the proposed
Second Amended Complaint appears to be an attempt to present argument as to the pending
Motion to Dismiss, which Plaintiff has already opposed (and successfully moved to vacate the
hearing as to). Additionally, allowing further amendment would be prejudicial to NCMEC, as
the proposed pleading—if allowed—would represent Plaintiff's fifth version of a complaint as to

this dispute.' In further support, NCMEC states as follows:

1 As detailed below, Plaintiff filed (1) his original complaint; (2) moved to amend that complaint, then
voluntarily dismissed the action when NCMEC opposed the motion to amend, while a motion to dismiss
was pending; (3) filed his original complaint in this action; (4) filed a first amended complaint; and (5)
seeks leave to file the second amended complaint.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 74 _ Filed 09/18/26 Page 2 of 7 PagelD# 753

I. PROCEDURAL SETTING

The above-captioned matter is the Pro Se Plaintiff’s second lawsuit arising out of the
same operative events. In the first, Marvelle J. Ballentine vy. NCMEC, et al., Case No. 1:26-cv-
01341-MSN-WBP (E.D. Va. 2026), NCMEC filed a motion to dismiss. Plaintiff opposed that
motion, which was set for a hearing on August 16, 2026 before the Honorable Michael S.
Nachmanoff. Plaintiff filed a motion for leave to file a “First Amended and Supplemental
Complaint” on July 26, 2026, which was opposed by NCMEC on July 29, 2026. In lieu of
allowing the Court to rule on either the Motion to Dismiss or the motion to amend the complaint,
Plaintiff voluntarily dismissed the action on the same day that NCMEC filed its opposition (July
29, 2026).

The following day, Plaintiff filed the original Complaint [Doc. 1] in this matter. Prior to
filing of any responsive pleading, Plaintiff filed a First Amended Complaint on August 6, 2026
[Doc. 5]. On August 12, 2026, Defendant the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children
filed a motion to dismiss [Doc. 10], which motion was joined by Defendant Hall on September 2,
2026 [Doc. 45]. Plaintiff has opposed both motions to dismiss via “Protective Oppositions.”
[Docs. 30, 51]

On September 8, 2026, Plaintiff filed the Motion at issue, his “Motion for Leave to File
Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint and Request for Expedited Determination on the
Papers.” [Doc. 59] While the First Amended Complaint was 260 paragraphs and 49 pages long,
the proposed “Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint” is 297 paragraphs and 50 pages

long, and would represent Plaintiff’s fifth attempt to set forth a claim as to the events at issue.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 74 _ Filed 09/18/26 Page 3 of 7 PagelD# 754

On September 9, 2026, the Court ordered Plaintiff to provide a redlined version of the proposed
Second Amended Complaint no later than September 11, 2026, which was to “clearly indicate
the changes, deletions, and additions that were made to Plaintiffs Complaint.” [Doc. 63] The
Order noted that the Court “does not possess sufficient information to issue an Order on this
matter.” [Id.]

Plaintiff did not file the redlined version of the proposed pleading as ordered. On
September 14, 2026, Plaintiff instead filed “Rule 72(a) Objections” to, inter alia, the Court’s
order to provide a redlined version of the proposed Second Amended Complaint, in which
Plaintiff objected to the redline requirement, the deadline imposed by the Court, and various
other orders. [Doc. 66] (NCMEC notes that Plaintiff represents that because he does not receive
notices of electronic filing, Plaintiff was unaware of the Order requiring a redline version of the
document until 9:00 P.M. on September 11, 2026.)

Il. STANDARD OF REVIEW

Under Rule 15(a), leave to amend is to be granted freely, “absent bad faith, undue
prejudice to the opposing party, or futility of amendment.” Hardee v. Mun. Jail Va. Beach
Sheriff's Off, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 184735, *5 (E.D. Va. 2025) (quoting United States v.
Pittman, 209 F.3d 314, 317 (4th Cir. 2000)); Save Our Sound OBX, Inc. v. N.C. DOT, 914 F.3d
213, 228 (4th Cir. 2019) (same). A proposed amendment is futile “when it is clearly insufficient
or frivolous on its face... [or] if the claim it presents would not survive a motion to dismiss.”
Id., United States ex rel. Wilson v. Kellogg Brown & Root, Inc., 525 F.3d 370, 375 (4th Cir.
2008). In determining futility, the Court is empowered to “apply common sense.” Nasim v.

Warden, Md. House of Corr., 64 F.3d 951, 954 (4th Cir. 1995).

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 74 _ Filed 09/18/26 Page 4 of 7 PagelD# 755

HI. ARGUMENT

As a threshold matter, NCMEC respectfully submits that the Motion should be denied
due to Plaintiff’s failure to comply with the Court’s Order to provide a redlined version of the
pleading. As noted, both the First Amended Complaint and proposed Second Amended
Complaint are approximately fifty pages long—and despite numerous efforts, undersigned
counsel has been unable to “reverse-engineer” a redline comparison of the two documents via
either Adobe or Word. That requirement is neither onerous, nor novel; while Plaintiff’s failure to
timely file the ordered document is understandable based on his representations as to not
receiving notifications, his refusal to do so is puzzling at best, as such a document would allow
the litigants and the Court the opportunity to easily see what changes have been made. Given the
procedural uncertainty due to Plaintiff’s objection to the Court’s order as to a redline version of
the document, and given the time constraints in which NCMEC is required to file an Opposition,
NCMEC requests the opportunity to supplement or amend this Opposition, if and when Plaintiff
submits the redline version of the proposed Second Amended Complaint.

Based on the representations in Plaintiff’s Memorandum in Support of the Motion for
Leave [Doc. 60], however, NCMEC respectfully submits that leave to amend at this stage would
be futile and unnecessary. In Plaintiffs’ Memorandum, he asserts that:

The SAC [Second Amended Complaint] does five principal things. First, the

SAC strengthens the falsity allegations in three respects... [and] pleads source-

level falsity concerning the asserted association between the two CyberTipline

reports and “Marvelle J. Ballentine”... pleads “person-level falsity” concerning

the implication that the reports concern Plaintiff personally... pleads defamation

by implication arising from the letters combined working and omitted

limitations... pleads that Plaintiff never used that name to create, identify, or

operate any Meta account... pleads, on information and belief, that neither report,

as NCMEC originally received it, identified Plaintiff by that name or concerned

Plaintiff personally. Second, the SAC pleads the distinction between the three

search identifiers Plaintiff supplied and the contents of the two reports. Third,
the SAC incorporates the post-filing events underlying Plaintiffs pending Rule

4

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 74 _ Filed 09/18/26 Page 5 of 7 PagelD# 756

15(d) motion... Fourth, the SAC pleads later statements and filings by

Defendants and their counsel... Those statements and filings bear on Defendants’

subsequent knowledge, continuing positions, and the unresolved reference of the

April 22, 2026 letters. Fifth, the SAC strengthens the factual allegations

supporting Counts J through VI without changing any count.

Doc. 60 at p. 2-3 (emphasis added for ease of review). Taking these arguments in order:

As to the first purported change, that is apparently in response to NCMEC’s pending
Motion to Dismiss, in which NCMEC asserts, inter alia, that the allegedly-actionable
statement—that NCMEC received CyberTipline Reports for any of the three identifiers in
Plaintiff’s subpoena to NCMEC—are true, and that Plaintiff cannot plausibly assert falsity,
because he does not have access to those reports. No allegations Plaintiff can make can change
that fact; if Plaintiff had access to the CyberTipline reports, they presumably would be exhibits to
the pleading, or provided under seal to the Court for review.

As to the second purported change, Plaintiff has filed “protective oppositions” to the
motions to dismiss, and fought against having a hearing held on NCMEC’s Motions to Dismiss.
He has had the opportunity to argue as to any distinctions he sees fit; there is no reason an
amended pleading is needed to accomplish that goal.

As to the third and fourth purported change, Plaintiff attempts to “incorporate post-filing
events underlying Plaintiff’s pending Rule 15(d) motion” and “later statements and filings by
Defendants and their counsel...” To be clear, no defendant has individually filed any document
in this matter—i.e., all filings have been by counsel— and it remains entirely unclear how an
argument in a motion to dismiss, or opposition to a motion, could form the basis of any pleading.

Plaintiff alleges that the fifth purported change “strengthens the factual allegations...

without changing any count.” Given the length of the proposed document, and the fact that the

format of the factual allegations have changed, it is unclear how the factual allegations have been

strengthened. However, this again appears to relate to argument as to the motions to dismiss,
which presumably were presented in the “protective oppositions,” or could have been presented
at a hearing, had Plaintiff not moved to have those hearings vacated.

Additionally, NCMEC respectfully submits that amendment would not impact the
arguments set forth in NCMEC’s pending Motions to Dismiss, and thus would be futile.
Specifically, NCMEC has argued that (1) the claims are barred by the litigation privilege, in that
the allegedly-actionable statements were made in a subpoena response; (2) that NCMEC has
statutory immunity to several of Plaintiff’s causes of action; (3) that Plaintiff cannot plausibly
assert that the statements are false, as he does not have access to the CyberTipline reports; (4) the
allegedly-defamatory meaning cannot be imputed from the language utilized in the statements at
issue; and (5) that the “insulting words” claim fails for the same reason. None of the broadly-
described changes impact those arguments, and as noted, Plaintiff has filed oppositions to those
motions and intentionally avoided the opportunity to present oral argument.

Finally, NCMEC respectfully submits that allowing leave to file a second amended
complaint would be prejudicial to NCMEC. As noted above, NCMEC has been forced to file
numerous motions in the prior iteration of this lawsuit, and in the present suit, and Plaintiff has
resisted on multiple occasions NCMEC’s opportunity to have the Court rule on motions to
dismiss. In the event that the Motion for Leave is granted, NCMEC will be forced to file a third
motion to dismiss, as to a dispute that NCMEC respectfully submits lacks merit. Given
Plaintiff’s multiple prior amendments—in this case and the prior iteration—NCMEC respectfully
submits that it will continue to suffer unfair prejudice if amendment is allowed prior to this

Honorable Court ruling on the pending motions to dismiss.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 74 _ Filed 09/18/26 Page 7 of 7 PagelD# 758

IV. CONCLUSION

In light of the foregoing, NCMEC respectfully submits that Plaintiff's Motion for Leave
to File a Second Amended Complaint be denied, on the basis of futility, or in the alternative that
the Motion be held in abeyance until the Court has had the opportunity to rule on the pending
Motions to Dismiss, in the event the Court believes that any defects in the pleadings could be

addressed via amendment.

Respectfully submitted,
